item.title: Judge orders officials to preserve Pike execution evidence
item.description:
A Tennessee judge ordered the state Wednesday to preserve all evidence related to the September 30 botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike. Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles granted the request at a status hearing after Pike’s attorneys argued that evidence from the failed attempt would be needed to challenge any future effort to execute her. “The state has made no promises that Miss Pike will not be subject to our future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes,” attorney Luke Ihnen argued. The order covers medical supplies used during the attempt — syringes, needles, tubing, and drugs — as well as the packaging labels that came with them and any notes from the medical professionals involved. item.title: France suspends stun grenade use at student protests after pupil loses hand
item.description:
French authorities suspended the use of stun grenades Wednesday after a teenager lost his hand during clashes with police, as demonstrations over school conditions spread to more than 40 cities. Protesters’ weekslong blockade of schools is the most visible aspect of a multifaceted national crisis, as public workers strike, bond yields rise to multidecade highs , and France’s traditional parties reckon with the far-right. But one proximate trigger of public discontent may have been overlooked: a ban on phones in schools enforced last month. Following the loss of this “comfort object” — which provides entertainment and connection — the “high school student has opened their eyes to a situation that has suddenly become unbearable ,” a French teacher argued in Grand Continent. — Brendan Ruberry

item.title: These state supreme court races could decide abortion access and trans rights
item.description:
Whoever wins state judicial races in November will not just be interpreting the law. They will be writing the next chapter of it. Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty Images In the heated news coverage of what’s at stake in the 2026 midterms , state supreme court races are drawing relatively little attention. Yet these are highly significant elections. Thirty-one states are holding supreme court elections in 2026, with voters nationwide picking judges to fill more than 60 open seats. As a law professor whose research and writing focuses on reproductive health , I’m watching these races closely. That’s because in the coming years these courts will have the final word on many consequential legal fights around abortion and trans healthcare. item.title: Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support before waking, lawyers say
item.description:
The death chamber in Huntsville, Texas Joe Raedle/Getty Images Over the course of two hours, witnesses watched and listened as Christa Pike cried, whimpered and snored through Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. By the end of it, executioners had given her two doses of the state’s lethal injection drugs. Her arms were swollen and blistered, and one had turned purple, her attorneys said. And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs. Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. item.title: Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
item.description:
Thousands of people joined a student march in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest against Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff. Bolsonaro led Sunday's first-round vote, prompting demonstrators to rally behind incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and oppose the far right's return to power.

item.title: Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear, Army study found
item.description:
A newly released military study paints a frightening picture of the electric shock gloves ICE recently purchased by the thousands—and which the agency and its acting head David Venturella seem eager to deploy regardless of the potential consequences. Records unearthed by the watchdog group American Oversight and first shared with the Associated Press show that in one set of trials carried out by the US Army in 2024, the electric shock gloves caused “overwhelmingly immediate” pain to soldiers playing the role of combative inmates in a mock forced cell extraction scenario, who then reported that “just seeing the glove” frightened them into obedience. GLOVEs, or Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, are taser-like devices that look like standard work gloves, but deliver a painful electric charge when the wearer touches a person’s skin. item.title: Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
item.description:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. The scenario is right out of a Stephen King novel: At a medical lab stashed away in a remote Siberian city, a pretty young technician was exposed to a deadly pathogen. She died, the lab went into lockdown , and soon rumors emerged that the Russian security services were on the scene. Now the world waits to see whether some monstrous microbe is going to make its way out of Russia’s forests. What’s going on in Russia is bad, but—at least so far—not that bad. We know that someone working at a research institute that studies various forms of plague has died of pneumonia, which suggests that she mishandled a sample of pneumonic plague. That’s about it.
